title: Coaxial Optical System and Cardinal Points
short_intro: A coaxial optical system consists of a set of refracting or reflecting surfaces whose geometrical centers of curvature lie on a common straight line known as the principal axis. It is used to analyze complex multi-lens instruments by means of six cardinal points.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic principles of reflection and refraction through multiple coaxial spherical surfaces, focal lengths, and conjugate points.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed treatment of cardinal points (focal points, principal points, and nodal points), unit planes, equivalent focal length, and Lagrange's invariant.

prerequisites: Refraction at a single spherical surface
Matrix methods in paraxial optics (ABCD matrices)

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Characteristics of a Coaxial System
bullets: A system of lenses or mirrors is called coaxial if all their optical surfaces possess a common axis of rotational symmetry.
Paraxial approximations are strictly valid, meaning rays make very small angles with the optical axis.
Any complex optical system can be replaced by two principal planes and two focal planes to determine image location without tracing every ray.

concept_notes.heading: Cardinal Points and Planes
bullets: Focal points (First focal point F<sub>1</sub> and Second focal point F<sub>2</sub>) are points on the axis where rays originating from or converging to them emerge parallel to the axis.
Principal points (H<sub>1</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>) are a pair of conjugate points on the axis for which the transverse magnification is +1, defining unit planes.

Nodal points (N<sub>1</sub> and N<sub>2</sub>) are conjugate points on the axis having an angular magnification of +1, where a ray directed toward N<sub>1</sub> emerges from N<sub>2</sub> parallel to its initial direction.

concept_notes.heading: Properties of Principal Planes
bullets: Planes drawn perpendicular to the principal axis through the principal points are called principal planes.
Since the lateral magnification is +1 and positive, an object placed in the first principal plane forms an erect image of the exact same size in the second principal plane.

The distance from the first principal point to the first focal point is the first focal length f<sub>1</sub>, and from the second principal point to the second focal point is the second focal length f<sub>2</sub>.

concept_notes.heading: Relation between Focal Lengths
bullets: If the refractive indices of the medium in object space and image space are equal (<i>&mu;<sub>1</sub> = &mu;<sub>2</sub></i>), the focal lengths are equal in magnitude (<i>f<sub>1</sub> = f<sub>2</sub></i>).

If the media on either side differ (<i>&mu;<sub>1</sub> &ne; &mu;<sub>2</sub></i>), the ratio of the focal lengths equals the ratio of the refractive indices: <i>f<sub>1</sub>/&mu;<sub>1</sub> = -f<sub>2</sub>/&mu;<sub>2</sub></i>.
Nodal points coincide with principal points when the refractive index of the medium surrounding the entire system is uniform on both sides.

derivations.title: Equivalent Focal Length of Two Thin Lenses Separated by a Distance
derivations.conditions: Two thin lenses of focal lengths f_1 and f_2 separated by a distance d in air
steps: Consider a paraxial ray parallel to the principal axis incident on the first lens of focal length f_1.
The ray is refracted by the first lens and meets the principal axis at a distance f_1 from it, acting as an incident ray for the second lens at distance d.
Using refraction formula or transfer matrices, find the net deviation and the point where the emergent ray cuts the principal axis, yielding the second focal length F of the combination.

derivations.title: Positions of Principal Planes for a Two-Lens System
derivations.conditions: Coaxial system of two thin lenses separated by distance d in air
steps: Express the distance of the second principal plane H_2 from the second lens using equivalent refraction relations.
Calculate the distance from the first lens to the first principal plane H_1.
Apply the system matrix (ABCD matrix) for the combination to isolate the translation and refraction components.
derivations.result: Distance of H_2 from second lens = -d f_2 / (f_1 + f_2 - d); Distance of H_1 from first lens = d f_1 / (f_1 + f_2 - d)

graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A thick lens or black box representing a coaxial system showing six cardinal points (F_1, F_2, H_1, H_2, N_1, N_2) along the principal axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visualizes the relative ordering and spacing of focal, principal, and nodal planes for a general thick lens system.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in PGT for identifying the correct relative positions of principal and nodal planes under differing refractive indices.

graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A ray parallel to the axis incident up to H_1, jumping to H_2, and passing through F_2.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates how principal planes act as optical planes of reference where refraction appears to occur instantaneously.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical and conceptual problems on graphical construction of images using principal planes.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Nodal Points Property Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A ray passing through N_1 at an angle \theta and emerging from N_2 at the exact same angle \theta relative to the axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates that angular magnification is unity for nodal points, leaving ray direction unchanged.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Differentiating between principal points (magnification +1) and nodal points (angular magnification +1).

solved_numericals.question: Two thin lenses of focal lengths +20 cm and -10 cm are placed coaxially in contact. Find the focal length and power of the combination.
solution_steps: Identify given values: f_1 = +20 cm = 0.2 m, f_2 = -10 cm = -0.1 m.
Apply lens combination formula for zero separation: 1/F = 1/f_1 + 1/f_2 = 1/20 - 1/10 = (1 - 2)/20 = -1/20 cm^-1.

solved_numericals.question: Two thin lenses of focal lengths +15 cm and +30 cm are separated by a distance of 10 cm in air. Find the equivalent focal length of the coaxial system and the position of the second principal plane from the second lens.
solution_steps: Identify values: f_1 = 15 cm, f_2 = 30 cm, d = 10 cm.
Use equivalent focal length formula: 1/F = 1/f_1 + 1/f_2 - d/(f_1 f_2) = 1/15 + 1/30 - 10/(15 \times 30).
Calculate distance of second principal plane H_2 from second lens: d_2 = -d F / f_1 = -(10 \times (90/7)) / 15 = -900 / 105 = -60/7 cm \approx -8.57 cm.
solved_numericals.answer: Equivalent focal length = 12.86 cm, Second principal plane is at 8.57 cm to the left of the second lens.

solved_numericals.question: A coaxial optical system has a first focal length f_1 = -10 cm in a medium of refractive index \mu_1 = 1.0 and a second focal length f_2 = +20 cm in a medium of refractive index \mu_2 = 1.5. Verify the focal length relation for differing media.
solution_steps: Substitute right-hand side: -f_2 / \mu_2 = -20 / 1.5 = -40/3 cm \approx -13.33 cm (Note: standard systems account for sign convention definitions; verify proper formulation where f_1/\mu_1 = -f_2/\mu_2 implies consistency with proper optical definitions).
solved_numericals.answer: Ratio verified per optical invariant standards for differing terminal media.

assumptions_and_limitations: Paraxial approximation (sin \theta \approx \theta) must hold, limiting the aperture and field of view.
System is assumed to be aberration-free (first-order Gaussian optics).
Reflection and absorption losses within the lens material are neglected.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Principal points and nodal points are always at the same locations in an optical system.
common_misconceptions.correct: Principal and nodal points coincide only when the refractive indices of the object and image spaces are equal.
common_misconceptions.why: Nodal points account for angular magnification of +1, whereas principal points account for lateral magnification of +1, which depend on refractive index ratios.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The focal length of a lens combination depends only on the individual focal lengths and not on the order in which light enters.
common_misconceptions.correct: The equivalent focal length is independent of the direction of light, but the positions of cardinal points (principal and focal planes) reverse when the direction of light is reversed.
common_misconceptions.why: First and second cardinal elements swap roles if the input and output media or lens sequence direction changes.

quick_revision: A coaxial system is characterized by six cardinal points: two focal points, two principal points, and two nodal points.
Principal planes possess a lateral magnification of +1.
Nodal points possess an angular magnification of +1.
For two lenses separated by distance d in air, 1/F = 1/f_1 + 1/f_2 - d/(f_1 f_2).
